content.title: Stop the decline and understand the current position
content.finding: The business's commercial base is declining, or no commercial base is forming at all.
content.consequence: The fundamental direction of the business right now is backward or nowhere — before anything else about strategy or execution matters, the business needs to stop losing ground or start gaining any at all.
content.action: Identify what's driving the decline (or the absence of any commercial base) and address it directly, with the immediate goal of reaching a flat, understood position rather than continued decline.
content.avoid: Launching several unrelated new initiatives at once to "try something" rather than diagnosing what's actually driving the decline first.
content.action_evidence: The commercial base is no longer declining — it's holding flat, even if growth hasn't started, and the drivers of the current position are understood.
content.assessment_evidence: Re-asked: is the commercial base flat, or is the direction at least known even without tracking showing growth? A "yes" answer (B) resolves this item.

content.title: Start tracking the commercial base and understand its drivers
content.finding: The commercial base is flat, or its direction isn't known because progress isn't tracked.
content.consequence: The business doesn't currently have forward momentum, or doesn't know if it does — either way, it can't currently say with confidence whether things are getting better.
content.action: Start tracking the commercial base consistently, and understand what's driving its current position — whether that means stabilizing it with understood drivers, or working toward growth, even if inconsistent so far.
content.avoid: Assuming growth is happening because the business feels busier, without actually tracking the commercial base itself.
content.action_evidence: The commercial base is being tracked, and its position — holding steady with understood drivers, or growing inconsistently — is known.
content.assessment_evidence: Re-asked: is the base holding steady with understood drivers, or growing even if inconsistently? A "yes" answer (C) resolves this item.

content.title: Turn inconsistent progress into a sustained growth trend
content.finding: The commercial base is holding steady with understood drivers, or growing inconsistently — real progress, but not yet a sustained growth trend.
content.consequence: The business hasn't yet demonstrated a real growth trend — an inconsistent pattern could turn back into flat or declining just as easily as it could become sustained growth, and right now there's no way to tell which.
content.action: Work toward consistent growth across more than one consecutive period, so the pattern becomes a demonstrated trend rather than an inconsistent one.
content.avoid: Declaring a single strong period a growth trend. The construct specifically requires more than one consecutive period — a trend test, not a one-off.
content.action_evidence: The commercial base has grown across more than one consecutive period.
content.assessment_evidence: Re-asked: is the commercial base growing across more than one consecutive period? A "yes" answer (D) resolves this item.

content.title: Start looking at some real figures
content.finding: No defined measures exist for tracking commercial progress — it's judged by impression rather than anything specific.
content.consequence: Whether the business believes it's doing well or poorly currently rests on a feeling rather than anything it could point to — impressions can be wrong in either direction, and there's no way to check them.
content.action: Start looking at some figures related to commercial progress, even if not yet consistently or against any stated expectation.
content.avoid: Looking at a figure once, drawing a conclusion, and not looking again for months. "Some figures looked at" still needs to happen with some regularity to count as progress.
content.action_evidence: Some figures relevant to commercial progress are being looked at, even without full consistency or a stated expectation to compare against.
content.assessment_evidence: Re-asked: are some figures looked at, even if not consistently or against an expectation? A "yes" answer (B) resolves this item.

content.title: Define and regularly track a small set of measures
content.finding: Some figures are looked at, but not consistently and not against any stated expectation.
content.consequence: The business is glancing at numbers without a defined discipline behind it — without consistency or a benchmark, it's hard to tell if a given figure is good, bad, or unremarkable.
content.action: Define a small set of measures that genuinely matter to this business's progress, and track them on a regular cycle.
content.avoid: Adopting a long list of measures because they're commonly tracked elsewhere, rather than a small set that's actually meaningful to this specific business.
content.action_evidence: A small, defined set of measures is tracked on a regular cycle.
content.assessment_evidence: Re-asked: is a small set of defined measures tracked on a regular cycle? A "yes" answer (C) resolves this item.

content.title: Make sure the tracked measures actually reflect this business's progress
content.finding: A small set of defined measures is tracked regularly, but they may be generic ones adopted because they're conventional, rather than the ones that genuinely reflect this business's own progress.
content.consequence: Tracking the wrong measures consistently gives a false sense of rigor — the business could be watching numbers that move for reasons unrelated to whether it's actually succeeding.
content.action: Review whether the tracked measures genuinely reflect this business's own progress, and replace any that don't with ones that do.
content.avoid: Adding more measures on top of the generic ones instead of replacing them. The goal is relevance, not volume.
content.action_evidence: The tracked measures are ones the business can specifically explain as reflecting its own progress, not generic industry defaults.
content.assessment_evidence: Re-asked: are the measures ones that genuinely reflect this business's progress, rather than generic ones? A "yes" answer (D) resolves this item.

content.title: Find out what growth is actually costing the business
content.finding: It isn't known what the business's growth costs it — the business doesn't examine what happens to its terms or existing base as it wins new business.
content.consequence: Growth could currently be happening at a real cost — worsening terms, or an eroding existing base — without the business having any visibility into whether that's the case.
content.action: Start examining what happens to terms and the existing customer base when the business wins new business, even if what's found isn't yet favorable.
content.avoid: Looking only at new business won while ignoring what's happening to the existing base at the same time. The construct is about both together.
content.action_evidence: The business has looked specifically at what its recent growth has cost it in terms and existing-base retention, and knows the answer, even if unfavorable.
content.assessment_evidence: Re-asked: is it known whether new business is being won on worse terms, or whether gains are offset by losses elsewhere? A "yes" answer (B, even if unfavorable) resolves this item.

content.title: Stop growth from eroding terms or the existing base
content.finding: New business is increasingly won on worse terms, or gains are being offset by losses elsewhere in the existing base.
content.consequence: The business's apparent growth may be costing more than it appears — deteriorating terms or an eroding base can make top-line growth look healthier than the underlying position actually is.
content.action: Address whatever is causing terms to worsen or the existing base to erode as the business grows, until terms and the existing base are broadly holding rather than deteriorating.
content.avoid: Accepting worse terms as "the cost of growth" without testing whether growth is actually achievable without conceding them.
content.action_evidence: Terms and the existing customer base are broadly holding steady as the business continues to grow.
content.assessment_evidence: Re-asked: are terms and the existing base broadly holding as the business grows? A "yes" answer (C) resolves this item.

content.title: Get evidence the business grows while holding terms and its base
content.finding: Terms and the existing base are broadly holding as the business grows, but this hasn't yet been evidenced — it's an impression rather than something the business can demonstrate.
content.consequence: Without evidence, the business can't confidently show that its growth is genuinely healthy rather than just currently appearing that way — a useful claim to be able to make to itself, and eventually to others.
content.action: Put together evidence that the business grows while maintaining its terms and retaining its existing base — specific figures or examples that could be shown, not just a general sense.
content.avoid: Relying on a single strong example as if it were evidence of a consistent pattern. The evidence needs to cover the growth and retention picture generally, not one anecdote.
content.action_evidence: The business can point to specific evidence that it maintains terms and retains its existing base while growing.
content.assessment_evidence: Re-asked: does the business grow while maintaining terms and retaining its existing base, with evidence for both? A "yes" answer (D) resolves this item.

content.title: Set objectives, even informally
content.finding: No objectives are set for the business.
content.consequence: Without stated objectives, there's no defined target the business is working toward — activity happens, but it isn't organized around anything specific enough to later assess.
content.action: Set objectives for the business, even loosely or informally, as a starting point — something specific enough to look back on later and ask whether it was met.
content.avoid: Setting objectives so vague ("grow the business," "do better") that they can't meaningfully be assessed as met or not later.
content.action_evidence: Objectives, even loose or informal ones, have been set for the business.
content.assessment_evidence: Re-asked: are objectives set loosely or informally, even if whether they're met isn't yet assessed? A "yes" answer (B) resolves this item.

content.title: Set specific objectives and assess whether they're met
content.finding: Objectives are set loosely or informally, but whether they were met is not assessed.
content.consequence: The business is setting intentions without ever closing the loop on whether they were achieved — objectives that are never assessed don't build any real discipline or learning over time.
content.action: Set specific objectives for a defined period, and assess at the end of that period whether they were met.
content.avoid: Assessing objectives only when they're obviously met, and quietly letting the ones that weren't fade without an honest look.
content.action_evidence: Specific objectives are set for a defined period, and the business has assessed whether they were met.
content.assessment_evidence: Re-asked: are specific objectives set for a defined period, with an assessment of whether they were met? A "yes" answer (C) resolves this item.

content.title: Build a track record of meeting objectives, or understanding why not
content.finding: Specific objectives are set and assessed, but there isn't yet a track record of meeting most of them, or a clear understanding of why not when they're missed.
content.consequence: The business is closing the loop on individual objectives, but hasn't yet built a pattern of reliably delivering on them, or a clear enough understanding of what causes the misses to correct course.
content.action: Build a track record of meeting most set objectives, and where they're missed, develop a clear understanding of why — not just that they were missed.
content.avoid: Attributing every missed objective to external circumstances without examining whether the objective itself, or the plan to reach it, was the real problem.
content.action_evidence: The business has a record of meeting most of its recent objectives, or a clear, specific understanding of why the ones it missed weren't met.
content.assessment_evidence: Re-asked: is there a record of meeting most objectives, or of clearly understanding why not? A "yes" answer (D) resolves this item.

content.title: Start building a repeatable activity alongside one-off progress
content.finding: Progress, where it exists, has come from one-off events — a single large order, a single introduction, a favourable moment — with no repeatable mechanism behind it.
content.consequence: The business's progress so far can't be counted on to continue, because nothing about how it happened is repeatable — it depended on circumstances that may not occur again.
content.action: Identify at least one activity behind recent progress that could plausibly be repeated, and begin repeating it, even if most progress still comes from one-off events for now.
content.avoid: Waiting for another favourable one-off event rather than actively building a repeatable activity in parallel.
content.action_evidence: At least one repeatable activity now exists and is contributing to progress, even if most progress still comes from one-off events.
content.assessment_evidence: Re-asked: does some repeatable activity exist, even if most progress still depends on one-off events? A "yes" answer (B) resolves this item.

content.title: Shift most progress onto the repeatable activity
content.finding: Some repeatable activity exists, but most progress still depends on one-off events.
content.consequence: The business has a repeatable mechanism in the mix, but it isn't yet doing the heavy lifting — most of what's driving progress is still things that happened once and may not happen again.
content.action: Shift effort toward the repeatable activity until most progress comes from it, rather than from one-off events.
content.avoid: Continuing to chase one-off opportunities as the primary strategy while treating the repeatable activity as a side project.
content.action_evidence: Most recent progress traces back to activity the business can and does repeat, rather than one-off events.
content.assessment_evidence: Re-asked: does most progress come from activity the business can and does repeat? A "yes" answer (C) resolves this item.

content.title: Prove the repeatable activity works more than once
content.finding: Most progress comes from repeatable activity, but it's only been done once in its current, effective form — it hasn't yet been repeated with comparable results.
content.consequence: A repeatable activity that's only worked once could still have been a fortunate first attempt — until it's been deliberately repeated, the business doesn't yet know if the results were the method working or a lucky first try.
content.action: Deliberately repeat the activity and confirm it produces comparable results more than once.
content.avoid: Changing the activity significantly each time it's attempted and calling that repetition. The point is confirming the same mechanism works again, not iterating to a different one each time.
content.action_evidence: The activity has been deliberately repeated, with comparable results, more than once.
content.assessment_evidence: Re-asked: has the activity been repeated deliberately, with comparable results more than once? A "yes" answer (D) resolves this item.
